Bitcoin has a public ledger, I don't think you can get around this with bitcoin alone.

An option is to dissolve BTC into an altcoin like Litecoin, send the payment as Litecoin, and have the receiver turn that litecoin back into bitcoin.
There is a public ledger, but nobody has to know the transaction is from me to Mike. Only way to tie the transaction to my person is to get end wallet divulge my name and email adress.
Anybody with the ability lean on whoever is exchanging dollars for bitcoins, on either end, and the inclination to, can pay attention to the block chain and figure it out.

The second you get bitcoin from anyone that has identifying information about you, you are no longer perfectly private. Spending bitcoin with anyone that has personal information about you is often a lesser encroachment on bitcoin privacy.

Or just convert money directly to litecoin. You don't have to go Bitcoin to litecoin anymore. You can go direct USD to anything relatively easily.

Edit: Mixed up a few words.

For starters, I think that it is totally irrelevant to the recent shooting and is only something that politicians can jump on to boost their popularity and make it seem like they're doing something, without addressing the real issues behind the shooting. Everything that I say is as a Southerner who was raised with enough Southern pride and heritage to make my grandmama proud. But I also do think that the Confederate flag does not belong on government buildings because of the historical link.

Now with that being said, there is also a lot of misinformation and kneejerk reactions about the Confederate flag. The flag that everyone thinks of as the Confederate flag was not the flag of the Confederate States of America; it was actually the battle flag of the Army of Northern Virginia, which was led by Robert E. Lee. That pattern was later adopted for use in the second and third national patterns, but it was never "officially" the flag of the CSA. After the war, the KKK and other white supremacist groups adopted the flag, and in 1948, the flag was a symbol for the States Rights Democratic Party, which was formed in opposition to the Civil Rights platform of the Democratic Party. The Confederate flag has the reputation that it does because it was usurped by white supremacists and neo-Nazis after the war.

Now also keep in mind that the United States as a whole has done some pretty atrocious things, including accepting slavery as law far longer than the CSA and almost committing genocide on the Native Americans. The United States' history is morally dubious and there are several actions that cannot be defended by even the most stalwart of patriots. However, the difference between the USA and CSA is that the United States was founded on the principles of liberty and equality, albeit with a lot of treason, bloodshed, and treachery (which is why calling the Southerners traitors is a very bad argument to be using), and the CSA was founded in defense of inequality and subjugation. Yes, states' rights were involved in the decision to secede, but ultimately, and what is widely regarded as the predominant reason to secede, the South seceded because of slavery (although it was viewed at the time as a states' rights issue), and the Confederate flag represents that decision.

However, banning the Confederate flag as a whole across the nation is not representative of free speech, which is protected by the constitution. The States are bound to protect your right to believe in whatever religious or political idea you have, be it the Flying Spaghetti Monster or Aryan race. So, as far as free speech goes, displaying the Confederate flag is acceptable, even if it is morally reprehensible. And honestly, most Southerners with Southern pride don't think of the Confederate flag as a symbol of oppression or slavery; it is a symbol of Southern pride and that is a huge part of their identity, so they fly it because they are proud to be Southern, not because they're necessarily racist or pro-slavery. It is an uneducated thing to do, but I can say that is genuinely where most people are coming from when they choose to fly or display a Southern flag. Now with that being said, the problem with flying the Confederate flag is because it is the equivalent of an American going to Vietnam and flying a flag at the My Lai massacre or a British person flying a Union Jack at the site of a Mau Mau prison camp. The Confederate flag holds that much, and more, historical baggage, and choosing to fly that flag as a symbol of Southern pride is only reminiscent of the oppression, persecution, and death of a large section of the American people. I don't support the idea that a government building should be flying a symbol that was based in that oppression and racism, as it puts a negative light on government and causes them to look biased towards a certain race or prejudiced idea, which government should not be.

To really eradicate the flag, we have to focus on education and giving Southerners something better to believe in or use to represent Southern pride (because trust me, Southern pride is not going away any time soon). Picking a symbol from the worst chapter of Southern history was a mistake and something that will take a while to remedy, but we have the chance to start that remedy, not by banning the flag as a whole, but by offering something different as a symbol of Southern pride from one of the good chapters of Southern history. I have no idea what that symbol could be, but I know that the Confederate flag is not it. In the meantime, we should focus on education and helping other people understand why the Confederate flag has the historical baggage that it does and why it is an offensive symbol to a lot of people.

So yes, I think the flag should be taken down from government buildings, as it is representative of the worst chapter in Southern history and is based in oppression of an entire race. But no, I don't think the flag should be banned, as it is still an expression of free speech, even if the people flying it are racist as fuck. But Southerners do have the huge opportunity to find something new to represent Southern pride that is not linked to oppression or racism. As a Southerner, I'm trying to figure out what that symbol would be, but hopefully by educating about the Confederate flag, what is really represents, and why it is such a historically loaded symbol to display, we can make a change for the better in the South.

First, let's establish who'd even seek out a mentor: people that want to become better, people with goals, and some motivation to see these goals through.

Now I'll provide an answer as to why at a certain point I stopped seeking advice of "successful" people. Specialization. Once I passed my early 20s, I had majority of life figured out. I can take care of my finances, I know how to acquire new skills, I've secured an education. Once my life education was complete, I no longer needed "life advice". Simply because every challenge that comes along is just a slight bump that is easily overcome. This would be true for any person seeking a mentor. Chances are they have their life together, since self-improvement and introspection are likely their chore characteristics.

This means that any life advice you have I don't need to seek out, sure if we're having a few pints and shooting the shit, you can tell me how you feel life should be lived. And then I'll tell you that everyone I know aims way too low, and I wish more people set their life trajectory much higher.

Aside from life, you also have specializations, which is actually something people will be interested in. Let's put aside Blogging and Women, your friends might be interested in these, but someone past the initial "life experience" stage can do both of those pretty easily. When you look at the other topics, Beekeeping, Chess, Languages, your experience may help a newbie, but likely not someone past the initial learning curve in these subjects. Basically, if I was friends with you, I'd hit you up for a coffee session to map out the basic structure of how you went about learning any one of these, and I may check up occasionally if I get stumped. But I wouldn't establish a mentor/mentee relationship for these subjects. I just don't believe your proficiency in them is high enough.

This leaves your primary specialization: Software Development. I've recently become interested in programming, but I wouldn't waste your time on my newbie questions, because Google can answer them. This means that I might do a coffee session to figure out how you got started in it, and then disappear as I get to moderate level of competence. And only once I am moderately good would I actually seek you out as a mentor if I wanted to keep pursuing this. But it sounds like you actually get paid to mentor good software developers already, so you know about this.

So as you can hopefully see, the type of person that would want to learn from you would likely either be a person who needs life advice, which means they are still rather young (think university age), or someone who has decided to pursue software development very seriously. Otherwise, your life experience will most likely benefit your friends who will ask you questions over coffee, beer, or a glass of orange juice.

But don't worry, your situation is not unique, it's true for a lot of others (successful people tend to specialize). It's why finding a mentor is actually pretty easy, the competition for their attention just isn't there. :)
